identification.summary: PassCV is a name first coined by Snorre Fagerland of Blue Coat Systems for a malware cluster; Cylance's SPEAR team later widened it to cover the malware and the APT group behind the larger C2 infrastructure and stolen Authenticode certificates [S1]. Cylance described the group as using many stolen code-signing certificates and as moving from older infrastructure to off-the-shelf RATs and custom code [S1]. Cylance said it identified eighteen previously undisclosed stolen certificates issued to companies and individuals in China, Taiwan, Korea, Europe, the United States and Russia [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Cylance's 2016-10-18 report is the main source. Cylance saw clues that more than one group might share the stolen certificates, but judged a single group using several public RATs more likely [S1]. The Blue Coat post that coined the name was not opened.

attribution.sponsor: The Council on Foreign Relations Cyber Operations Tracker lists China as the suspected state sponsor [S3]. Cylance, in the text reviewed, names no government sponsor [S1].
attribution.confidence: Low. The only sponsor statement found is a CFR tracker entry listing suspected Chinese sponsorship [S3]. Cylance noted that several groups might share the certificates [S1].
attribution.basis: CFR tracker entry [S3]. No technical attribution to a state organization was found in the sources reviewed.

objectives: Cylance reported malware aimed at game developers, with code to harvest stored passwords and log keystrokes [S2]. The custom Saber RAT could hijack and steal in-game account information and items [S2]. The CFR entry says the actor stole digital certificates from game companies for use against other targets [S3]. The overall objective is not stated by the sources; the activity as described mixes data theft, theft of signing certificates and in-game asset theft.

sectors: Online video game developers and platforms [S2][S3]
regions: Certificate owners were in China, Taiwan, Korea, Europe, the United States and Russia [S1]
CFR lists suspected victim countries China, Taiwan, South Korea, the United States and Russia [S3]
targeting.notes: Infosecurity Magazine reports the group went after developers using the Unity engine and Cocos2d framework; the Pokemon Go reference in the headline is only an example of a Unity game and does not say that game was attacked [S2]. Phony resumes and CVs were used to deliver backdoors [S2].

capabilities.summary: Heavy use of stolen Authenticode certificates to sign malware [S1]. Obfuscated and signed versions of older RATs such as ZxShell and Ghost RAT [S2], plus a custom RAT called Saber with DDoS and in-game account theft functions [S2]. Cylance said the group began expanding into other off-the-shelf RATs and custom code, and noted a move into signed adware [S1][S2]. Delivery used phony resumes and CVs [S2].

campaigns.name: Signed malware targeting gaming companies
campaigns.summary: Cylance SPEAR published findings on eighteen new stolen certificates, C2 infrastructure and new custom RATs, with a cluster of activity aimed at game developers. CFR logged the incident in October 2016.

diamond.adversary: Unattributed; CFR lists suspected Chinese sponsorship, and Cylance leaned to a single group while noting possible certificate sharing [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: Stolen-certificate code signing; signed ZxShell, Ghost RAT and other RATs; custom Saber RAT; credential harvesting and keylogging [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Cylance described a large C2 infrastructure tied together with the stolen certificates; specific indicators were not reviewed [S1].
diamond.victim: Online game developers and platforms; certificate owners across several countries [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints that trust Authenticode-signed binaries; game engines such as Unity and Cocos2d as developer targets [S1][S2].

gaps: Fetching failed for every page tried (connection errors), so all content comes from search-result summaries; Cylance/BlackBerry, Infosecurity Magazine and CFR pages were not read in full.
The original Blue Coat (Fagerland) post that coined PassCV was not located; first-observed date unknown.
No government attribution or named operators found; the CFR China-sponsor entry is the only sponsor statement and its basis was not reviewed.
No activity after 2016 found in sources reviewed.
ETDA and Malpedia profiles exist but were not opened and carry no date seen; aliases are not confirmed by a cited source.
Infosecurity Magazine publication date was not seen; 2016-10 is inferred from its coverage of the Cylance report.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Code-signing trust and software-development environments are key terrain; stolen certificates let malware appear legitimate [S1]. STEP 2: Signed binaries can defeat reputation-based allowlisting [S1]. STEP 3: The observed pattern is resume or CV lure, then signed RAT, then credential and keystroke theft [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued theft of certificates and credentials from software developers. MDCOA is use of a stolen certificate from a defense software vendor to sign tooling aimed at DoD-adjacent targets. Candidate indicators: unexpected signed binaries from certificate owners that do not match the software, and ZxShell or Ghost RAT network behavior [S1][S2]. The sources describe gaming targets only, so relevance to DoD is an inference.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track revoked or abused code-signing certificates and feed them to allowlisting policy. (2) Authorities: certificate revocation and blocking requests run through the owning vendor and CAs rather than DoD authorities. (3) Mission assurance: do not treat a valid signature as proof of trust for software in contractor or developer pipelines. (4) Coordination: share indicators through DC3 and the commercial vendor community. Evidence is dated 2016 and thin.

provenance.importedSummary: The PassCV group continues to be one of the most successful and active threat groups that leverage a wide array of stolen Authenticode-signing certificates. Snorre Fagerland of Blue Coat Systems first coined the term PassCV in a blog post. His post provides a good introduction to the group and covers some of the older infrastructure, stolen code-signing certificate reuse, and other connections associated with the PassCV malware. There are several clues alluding to the possibility that multiple groups may be utilizing the same stolen signing certificates, but at this time SPEAR believes the current attacks are more likely being perpetrated by a single group employing multiple publicly available Remote Administration Tools (RATs). The PassCV group has been operating with continued success and has already started to expand their malware repertoire into different off-the-shelf RATs and custom code. SPEAR identified eighteen previously undisclosed stolen Authenticode certificates. These certificates were originally issued to companies and individuals scattered across China, Taiwan, Korea, Europe, the United States and Russia. In this post we expand the usage of the term ‘PassCV’ to encompass the malware mentioned in the Blue Coat Systems report, as well as the APT group behind the larger C2 infrastructure and stolen Authenticode certificates. We’d like to share some of our findings as they pertain to the stolen certificates, command and control infrastructure, and some of the newer custom RATs they’ve begun development on.
